summary: Given capacities, current rocks and extra rocks, return the maximum number of bags that can be made full.
mainInsight: Each bag costs (capacity - rocks) to fill and filling it gives one full bag. Spend the extra rocks on the cheapest bags first.
invariant: After handling the first i sorted needs, the rocks left are the best possible for filling i bags.

approaches.name: Subset search
approaches.summary: Try all subsets of bags and keep those whose total need fits.

approaches.name: Greedy on sorted needs
approaches.summary: Sort needs ascending; subtract while the budget allows.

personalSolution.approach: Sort the needs and fill from the smallest
personalSolution.notes: Optimal. The branch for need == 0 is correct because zeros sort first; a simple `if need > rocks: break` loop is shorter.

commonMistakes: Partially filling bags, which gains nothing.
edgeCases: More extra rocks than total need.
Fewer rocks than the smallest need.

promptVariants: Which technique solves this problem, and what in the statement or constraints points to it?
Name the technique you would use here and the clue in the problem that tells you.
What approach fits this problem, and which part of the statement gives it away?
cards.answer: Greedy: sort the number of rocks each bag is missing and fill the smallest needs first. Clue: A bag only counts when it is completely full and filling it costs its missing rocks, so to maximise the number of full bags we should spend the extra rocks on the cheapest bags first.
keyPoints: A bag only counts when it is completely full and filling it costs its missing rocks, so to maximise the number of full bags we should spend the extra rocks on the cheapest bags first.
cards.explanation: This is a selection problem with item costs and a budget; picking the cheapest items first maximises the count.

rubric.technique: Greedy: sort the number of rocks each bag is missing and fill the smallest needs first

alsoValid.name: Try every subset of bags
alsoValid.note: correct, but exponential in the number of bags

rubric.clue: A bag only counts when it is completely full and filling it costs its missing rocks, so to maximise the number of full bags we should spend the extra rocks on the cheapest bags first.

promptVariants: Why is filling the bags with the smallest need first optimal?
Give the exchange argument for the greedy choice.
cards.answer: Each bag has a cost (capacity - rocks) and gives one unit of value if it is filled completely. Suppose an optimal solution fills a bag with cost b but skips a cheaper bag with cost a <= b. Swapping them keeps the number of full bags and frees b - a rocks, so filling the cheapest bags first is never worse. Partial filling is wasted, so only whole-bag costs matter.
keyPoints: Cost of a bag = missing rocks
Swapping a costlier bag for a cheaper one is never worse
cards.explanation: Maximising a count under a budget is solved by taking the cheapest items first.

promptVariants: Why is processing the bags in their original order wrong?
Which input defeats filling bags in index order?
options: With needs [4, 1, 1, 1] and 3 rocks, index order fills none while sorting fills three
With needs [1, 1, 1, 4] and 3 rocks, index order fills one while sorting fills three
With needs [2, 2, 2, 2] and 4 rocks, index order fills one while sorting fills two
With needs [1, 2, 3, 4] and 6 rocks, index order and sorting both fill three
cards.answer: With needs [4, 1, 1, 1] and 3 rocks, index order fills none while sorting fills three
cards.explanation: The first bag needs 4 > 3 rocks, so an in-order greedy stops immediately, while sorted needs [1, 1, 1, 4] let three cheap bags be filled.

incorrectOptionExplanations.With needs [1, 1, 1, 4] and 3 rocks, ind: In index order the first three bags are the cheap ones, so it also fills three.
incorrectOptionExplanations.With needs [2, 2, 2, 2] and 4 rocks, ind: Equal needs make the order irrelevant; both fill two bags.
incorrectOptionExplanations.With needs [1, 2, 3, 4] and 6 rocks, ind: True, but it is not a counterexample: the order is already sorted.

promptVariants: Your loop condition is `while additionalRocks > 0`. Why does it not miss bags that are already full?
What guarantees that stopping when additionalRocks reaches 0 is safe in your loop?
cards.answer: After sorting ascending, all bags with need 0 come first and are counted before any rocks are spent, so the loop reaches them while additionalRocks is still positive (the constraints give additionalRocks >= 1). Once additionalRocks becomes 0, every remaining bag has need > 0 and cannot be filled, so stopping is safe.
cards.explanation: The sort order is what makes the early stop correct.

promptVariants: What is the time complexity of the canonical code?
Which step dominates the running time?
options: O(n log n), dominated by the sort
O(n), one pass over the bags
O(n log n), from a heap of all needs
cards.answer: O(n log n), dominated by the sort
cards.explanation: Building the needs is linear and the greedy loop is linear after sorting; the sort costs O(n log n).

incorrectOptionExplanations.O(n), one pass over the bags: The sort of the needs adds a log factor.
incorrectOptionExplanations.O(n^2), comparing every pair: No pair is compared; the sort handles the ordering.
incorrectOptionExplanations.O(n log n), from a heap of all needs: No heap is used; a plain sort is simpler.

promptVariants: The sorted list of needs has one entry per bag, so the extra space is O(___).
cards.explanation: One stored need per bag; sorting in place would not change that.
